content: Cyclamate is an artificial sweetener that was first discovered in 1937 at the University of Illinois by a graduate student named Michael Sveda. Its discovery was accidental. Sveda was working in a laboratory on the synthesis of an anti-fever medication when he placed his cigarette on the lab bench. Upon putting the cigarette back in his mouth, he noticed a sweet taste, which led to the identification of cyclamate. The patent for cyclamate was initially purchased by DuPont but was later sold to Abbott Laboratories. Abbott conducted the necessary studies and submitted a New Drug Application in 1950. The company intended to use cyclamate to mask the bitterness of certain medications, such as antibiotics and pentobarbital. In 1958, cyclamate was classified as Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS) in the United States. It was marketed in tablet form as a sugar substitute for diabetics and also in liquid form. One such product, called Sucaryl, is still available in markets outside the United States. Cyclamate is 30 to 50 times sweeter than sugar, depending on its concentration, as the sweetness does not increase linearly with concentration. Some individuals report an unpleasant aftertaste, though it is generally less pronounced than that of saccharin or acesulfame potassium. Cyclamate is often used in combination with other artificial sweeteners, particularly saccharin, in a ratio of 10 parts cyclamate to 1 part saccharin. This combination helps to mask the off-tastes of both sweeteners. Cyclamate is less expensive than most other sweeteners, including sucralose, and it remains stable when exposed to heat. Chemically, cyclamate is the sodium or calcium salt of cyclamic acid, also known as cyclohexanesulfamic acid. It is synthesized through the sulfonation of cyclohexylamine, which can be achieved by reacting cyclohexylamine with either sulfamic acid or sulfur trioxide. In 1966, a study revealed that certain intestinal bacteria could desulfonate cyclamate, converting it into cyclohexylamine, a compound suspected of having chronic toxicity in animals. Further research in 1969 demonstrated that a mixture of cyclamate and saccharin in a 10:1 ratio increased the incidence of bladder cancer in rats. Specifically, eight out of 240 rats fed this mixture at levels equivalent to a human consuming 350 cans of diet soda per day developed bladder tumors. Additional studies implicated cyclohexylamine in causing testicular atrophy in mice. On October 18, 1969, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), citing the Delaney Amendment, banned the sale of cyclamate in the United States. The United Kingdom followed with a similar ban the following year. Abbott Laboratories contested these findings, claiming that their own studies failed to replicate the 1969 results. In 1973, Abbott petitioned the FDA to lift the ban on cyclamate, but this request was denied in 1980 by FDA Commissioner Jere Goyan. A second petition was filed in 1982 by Abbott Laboratories in collaboration with the Calorie Control Council, a lobbying group representing the diet food industry. Although the FDA has stated that a review of all available evidence does not implicate cyclamate as a carcinogen in mice or rats, the sweetener remains banned in food products in the United States. The petition to lift the ban is currently held in abeyance, meaning it is not actively being considered. It is unclear whether this is due to a request from Abbott Laboratories or because the FDA considers the petition insufficient. Cyclamate, however, is approved for use as a sweetener in over 55 countries. For example, the Canadian version of the brand-name sweetener Sweet'N Low contains cyclamate, whereas the U.S. version does not. Similarly, the Canadian version of Sugar Twin contains cyclamate, while the U.S. version contains saccharin. Animal studies have reported that cyclamate may cause irreversible testicular atrophy and affect the function of the seminal vesicles in mice and primates. However, the potential negative effects of cyclamate on male reproductive health may not fall within the scope of safety evaluations that focus solely on life expectancy and cancer risk. Interestingly, a reduction in testosterone levels, which cyclamate may cause, is associated with a lower incidence of certain cancers, such as testicular cancer, and an increased life expectancy. This could make it easier for a substance that impairs testosterone production to be classified as safe under these criteria. Since cyclamate appears to affect cells involved in sperm production, there is also concern that it might damage male reproductive DNA. However, there is currently no direct evidence to confirm or refute this possibility. Cyclamate is sold under various brand names in different countries, including Assugrin (Switzerland, Brazil), Sucaryl, and Sugar Twin (Canada).
